summary: This paper proposes Hessian-Enhanced Token Attribution (HETA), a post-hoc token attribution framework for decoder-only autoregressive language models that combines attention rollout semantic flow, Hessian-based second-order sensitivity, and KL-divergence information loss under token masking. The authors also introduce a 2,000-instance curated dataset combining NarrativeQA and SciQ contexts to evaluate attribution alignment using a proposed Dependent Sentence Attribution (DSA) metric. While the idea of unifying structural, geometric, and information-theoretic signals is conceptually interesting, the manuscript suffers from fundamental mathematical flaws in its Hessian formulation, unexplained order-of-magnitude empirical anomalies, and conceptual errors in its evaluation protocol.
strengths: Combines structural attention rollout, second-order Hessian curvature, and information-theoretic KL divergence into a multi-faceted attribution score tailored for decoder-only autoregressive models.
Introduces a curated 2,000-instance evaluation dataset (NarrativeQA + SciQ) along with the Dependent Sentence Attribution (DSA) metric to evaluate attribution precision against distractor context.
Evaluates across multiple decoder-only model architectures and parameter scales (GPT-J 6B, Phi-3 14B, LLaMA-3.1 70B, Qwen2.5 3B) across established benchmarks (LongRA, TellMeWhy, WikiBio).
Includes detailed component ablations and stress tests for sensitivity and active/passive syntactic rephrasing robustness.

key_concerns.issue: Mathematical flaw in Eq. 3 (Hessian Sensitivity): Eq. 3 samples Rademacher vectors r_k supported solely on block i (Π_i r_k = r_k) and projects back onto block i, which isolates the diagonal block H_{i,i} = ∇^2_{e_i, e_i} log P(x_T | x_{<T}). This measures only self-curvature of token i's embedding, NOT cross-token second-order interactions (H_{i,j}), directly contradicting claims throughout the paper that HETA captures second-order token-token interactions.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Correct the mathematical formulation and text: either revise Eq. 3 to explicitly measure off-diagonal cross-block curvature H_{i,j} (e.g., via joint HVPs between input token positions), or accurately re-scope all claims in the paper to state that Eq. 3 measures local self-curvature rather than inter-token interactions.

key_concerns.issue: Unexplained order-of-magnitude empirical anomalies in Table 3: On benchmark datasets, HETA achieves Soft-NC scores of 10.3 and 9.2 (GPT-J) and 9.9 (LLaMA-3.1), whereas all baseline methods range between 0.13 and 2.05. A 5x to 50x leap over all prior work without explanation suggests potential differences in attribution score normalization or metric evaluation code between HETA and baselines.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Provide a detailed analysis explaining the exact scale and magnitude of Soft-NC scores, verify that baseline attributions were normalized identically under the perturbation benchmark protocol, and release exact evaluation scripts for verification.

key_concerns.issue: Conceptual flaw in decoding hyperparameter sensitivity evaluation (Table 2): Evaluating post-hoc attribution sensitivity across decoding parameters (temperature, top-p, top-k, repetition penalty) is conceptually unclear because conditional log-probabilities P(x_T | x_{<T}) and model gradients on a fixed text sequence are independent of decoding parameters used during generation.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Clarify whether sequences were re-generated under each hyperparameter set (which alters the evaluation target text) or if attributions were evaluated on fixed text; if on fixed text, explain why decoding parameters would cause baseline attributions to fluctuate.

key_concerns.issue: Incomplete baseline reporting in Table 3 and missing computational cost analysis: In Table 3, ReAgent is reported for LLaMA-3.1 70B but omitted from GPT-J 6B and Phi-3 14B rows, despite being cited as the primary runner-up baseline in the text. Furthermore, the paper lacks wall-clock runtime, memory overhead, and backpropagation pass counts for computing Hutchinson HVPs and KL forward passes.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Include ReAgent across all models in Table 3 for consistency, and provide explicit runtime, memory, and FLOPS benchmarks comparing HETA (and its HETA-LR+WIN variant) against gradient and attention baselines.

questions_for_authors: How does Eq. 3 isolate cross-token interaction H_{i,j} when the projection Π_i restricts both the vector perturbation r_k and the output to block i, yielding only the diagonal block H_{i,i}?

Why are HETA's Soft-NC values in Table 3 (e.g., 10.3 vs 1.54) an order of magnitude higher than all baselines across every dataset and model? Were attribution magnitudes normalized differently prior to applying input perturbations?

In Table 2, how were decoding hyperparameters applied during post-hoc attribution? If the sequence x_{1:T} is fixed, how do temperature or top-p affect gradients or attention weights of P(x_T | x_{<T})?
Why was ReAgent omitted from the GPT-J 6B and Phi-3 14B results in Table 3 while being included for LLaMA-3.1 70B and in Table 1?
What is the exact wall-clock time and memory overhead per sequence of computing m HVPs and T masked forward passes for HETA compared to Integrated Gradients and ContextCite?
calibration_check: The claims are significantly overscoped, as the paper claims to model second-order token-token interactions despite Eq. 3 computing only single-token diagonal self-curvature (H_{i,i}), and claims unprecedented SOTA attribution performance without accounting for metric scale discrepancies or computational overhead.

significance.justification: Attributing outputs in decoder-only LLMs is an important problem for ICLR, but mathematical flaws and empirical anomalies reduce the immediate utility of the proposed method.

novelty.justification: Combining attention rollout, second-order Hessian sensitivity, and KL information loss is a novel unified concept, though individual components build on existing literature.

rigor.justification: The mathematical formulation in Eq. 3 extracts only diagonal block self-curvature (H_{i,i}) rather than token-token interaction (H_{i,j}), invalidating core theoretical claims.

statistical_soundness.justification: Results display unexplained order-of-magnitude jumps in Soft-NC scores (10.3 vs ~1.0) and rely on a conceptually ambiguous decoding hyperparameter experiment.

calibration_honesty.justification: The paper overclaims modeling second-order token interactions when Eq. 3 computes self-curvature, and claims massive performance gains without addressing metric calibration or computational cost.

clarity.justification: The manuscript is generally readable and structured well, but key mathematical equations are imprecise and critical experimental details are deferred to unprovided appendix sections.

structure_compliance.justification: The paper strictly adheres to standard conference formatting and section organization (Abstract, Introduction, Motivation, Method, Experiments, Related Work, Conclusion).

reproducibility.justification: Essential implementation details such as Hutchinson estimator sample counts, low-rank approximation parameters, and exact KL masking protocols are insufficiently detailed in the main text.

related_work.justification: The paper provides a solid overview of feature attribution, attention rollout, and recent LLM attribution methods, though baseline comparisons in tables are inconsistently formatted.

figure_quality.justification: Table captions and figure schematics clearly explain the proposed workflow and experimental setups, though Table 3 suffers from missing baseline rows.

breadth_generality.justification: Experiments cover four model families (GPT-J, Phi-3, LLaMA-3.1, Qwen2.5) across multiple tasks (LongRA, TellMeWhy, WikiBio, SciQ/NarrativeQA), offering reasonable coverage.

overall_recommendation.justification: Despite an ambitious goal and a useful curated dataset, fundamental mathematical errors in the Hessian formulation and severe empirical anomalies prevent acceptance in its current form.
